title: Tiffin Run
hook: You started a tiffin delivery startup in one city. Dispatch is a WhatsApp group. At 12:30 you get 40 orders a minute and 15 delivery partners, and your notes app is on fire.
context: Single-city tiffin delivery startup moving from WhatsApp dispatch to an app.
solution_brief: Decouple order acceptance from dispatch with a queue, make consumers idempotent, narrow the partner search with a spatial index, protect status with a state machine, and bound every wait with timeouts. Accept fast, dispatch asynchronously. Idempotent assignment keyed by order id. Geohash or grid cells, plus neighbouring cells. State machine with sequence numbers for status. Offer timeouts, next-candidate fallback, capped retries.

steps.prompt: The place-order API finds a delivery partner and waits for them to accept before replying, so at lunch the app hangs and customers tap Order again and again. How should the flow change?
steps.context_note: The order API is slow because it waits on a human to respond.

options.text: Raise the API timeout to 5 minutes so dispatch has time to finish
Add more API servers so more requests can wait on partners at once
Disable the Order button for 60 seconds after each tap
Save the order, reply at once, and dispatch from a queue

steps.explanation: Accepting an order is fast and certain, while finding a partner is slow and uncertain, so a queue between them gives customers instant confirmation and lets dispatch retry at its own pace. A longer timeout or more servers just hold more requests open behind a spinner, and disabling the button hides the symptom without fixing the wait.
steps.bottleneck_note: Do not make a fast user-facing request wait on a slow, uncertain background process.

steps.prompt: The queue delivers each message at least once. A worker crashes after assigning a partner but before acknowledging, so the order is dispatched again and two partners arrive with the same tiffin. How do you prevent double assignment?
steps.context_note: The queue is in place, but 'at least once' means duplicates happen.

options.text: Make assignment idempotent with a unique constraint on order_id
Delete each message from the queue before the worker starts processing it
Run a single dispatch worker so that two workers never overlap on an order
Raise the queue's visibility timeout so messages are never redelivered

steps.explanation: With at-least-once delivery, duplicates are normal, so the consumer must tolerate them: a unique constraint makes the second attempt fail harmlessly. Deleting the message first turns this into at-most-once, which loses orders when a worker crashes, and a single worker or longer timeout only narrows the crash window without closing it.
steps.bottleneck_note: Design consumers to be safe under redelivery instead of trying to prevent redelivery.

steps.prompt: What speeds up finding the closest free partner while still returning nearby ones?
steps.context_note: Dispatch is now correct, but the city has grown to 5,000 active partners and each order scans all of them.

options.text: Buy a faster server and keep scanning every partner for each order
Bucket partners into geohash cells; search the order's cell and neighbours
Offer the order to whichever partner finished a delivery most recently, wherever they are
Reuse the partner who was nearest to this customer's previous order

steps.explanation: A spatial index limits the search to partners near the customer, and neighbouring cells must be checked because the nearest partner may sit just across a boundary. A faster server still scans linearly with city size at lunch peak, and the last-free or previous-nearest shortcuts are quick but ignore where the partner is now.
steps.bottleneck_note: Turn a global scan into a local lookup with a spatial index.

steps.prompt: Customers sometimes see DELIVERED and then PICKED_UP. What stops that?
steps.context_note: Status updates from partner phones travel over weak mobile networks and do not arrive in the order they were sent.

options.text: Always apply the most recently received update
Order the updates by the timestamp recorded on each partner phone's own clock
Allow only legal transitions and ignore updates with a stale sequence number
Make partner apps resend each status every few seconds until the order closes

steps.explanation: Arrival order is not event order, so a state machine says DELIVERED cannot be followed by PICKED_UP and a per-order sequence number lets the server drop old updates. 'Latest received wins' is exactly the bug being seen, and phone clocks drift, so their timestamps cannot order events reliably.
steps.bottleneck_note: Never assume messages arrive in the order they were sent.

steps.prompt: The nearest partner is busy and never answers, so the order sits unassigned. What should dispatch do?
steps.context_note: Partners are people, and the nearest one has not responded to the offer.

options.text: Wait for the partner to answer
Time out the offer after 30 seconds and try the next candidate, with a cap
Cancel the order and refund the customer after the first non-response
Re-send the same offer to that partner every few seconds until they finally reply

steps.explanation: A timeout turns an open-ended wait into a bounded step, moving to the next candidate keeps the order flowing, and an attempt cap lets a human step in when nobody accepts. Waiting or nagging the same partner leaves the order stuck, and cancelling after one silent partner throws away a sale.
steps.bottleneck_note: Every external wait needs a timeout, a fallback and an upper bound on retries.
